$comment: THE CROSS-REPO CONTRACT. Every invariant that spans capucor-web, capucor-os and
capucor-docs, in one machine-readable place instead of prose in two AGENTS.md files.
WHY IT EXISTS. The 2026-08-04 audit kept finding the same four classes of drift —
coupled dependencies, the provisioning/schema contract, backup coverage, and files
duplicated on purpose — and every single one was caught by a person noticing, not by
anything failing. Drift that only a careful reader catches is drift that ships.
HOW IT IS ENFORCED. `capucor-os/scripts/audit-cross-repo.mjs` (npm run audit) reads
this file and checks every class against all three repos. It is READ-ONLY: it changes
nothing, writes nothing, and touches no production state.
WHY THREE COPIES. capucor-docs holds the canonical copy; capucor-web and capucor-os
each carry a byte-identical vendored copy under contracts/. A CI job runs in ONE
repo's checkout and cannot see its siblings, so a vendored copy is the only way the
in-repo test (src/__tests__/cross-repo-contract.test.ts) can enforce anything from
here. The cross-repo audit compares the three copies to each other, so a drifted copy
is caught by the same command it belongs to. Edit the capucor-docs copy first.

coupledDependencies.why: Next, OpenNext and Wrangler are a runtime TRIPLE, not three independent packages: OpenNext 1.20.x requires Next >=16.2.11, and moving one side alone can make a clean install select an adapter whose Next peer range the app does not satisfy. React and supabase-js are shared because both Workers render the same components and speak to the same PostgREST. All are pinned EXACT (no caret) on purpose — PH-01 pinned them after an unverified runtime pair shipped.

node.why: The dev box runs Node 24 / npm 11. CI ran Node 20 until 2026-08-03 and a lockfile written by npm 11 was rejected outright by npm 10. `.nvmrc` and the `setup-node` step in ci.yml must move together or that trap returns.

provisioning.why: A client signs on capucor.com and capucor-web starts a write whose schema lives in capucor-os. A rename on either side produces NO compile error and NO failing test in either repo. The symptom is a paying client whose durable portal stage keeps retrying.
provisioning.blindSpot: Since migration 017 an `after insert` trigger (client_orgs_default_entity -> ensure_default_entity) runs INSIDE the provisioning insert. If it ever raises, the insert aborts and a paying client gets no portal access. The two UNIT tripwires cannot see this and never will — one drives an in-memory fake, the other reads table invariants out of the migration text; both stay green against a trigger that raises on every insert. That is a permanent property of what they are, not a gap to close.
provisioning.blindSpotCleared: CLEARED — and it is covered continuously, so this is not outstanding work. (1) PO-01 proved it live on 2026-08-03: a throwaway org inserted into production `client_orgs` over PostgREST with the exact column shape provisionFromSignedProposal uses, one `is_primary` entity created, all eight name/reg/tax fields copied, cascade clean on delete — 22 checks, 0 failures. (2) Migration 018 then altered the function (`set search_path = ''`), which by PO-01's own rule required re-proving. (3) `capucor-os/e2e/global-setup.ts` re-proves it on EVERY run of `npm run e2e`: it inserts a real fixture org and THROWS BY NAME ('migration 017's ensure_default_entity trigger did not fire') if the default entity is not there. It ran green on 2026-08-05, after 018. That is why it is listed as a third tripwire above.
provisioning.blindSpotWatchOut: The e2e suite is deliberately NOT in CI (npm ci + a browser download on every push), so this coverage is real but on-demand. Re-run `npm run e2e` after any change to `entities`, to `ensure_default_entity()`, or to the trigger — that is now the live seam test, replacing the hand-run SQL in PO-01's Verify section.

handSynced.why: These files exist in both app repos and a one-sided edit costs money or breaks a seam, with no compile error and no failing test. The per-repo digests below are what lets a SINGLE repo's CI notice a one-sided edit: change the file, the digest moves, that repo goes red naming its counterpart. Regenerate the values with `npm run audit -- --print-digests` in capucor-os and paste them into all three copies of this file.

pairModes.byte: The two copies must be identical after whitespace normalisation.
pairModes.code: The two copies must be identical after comments and blank lines are stripped. Each repo keeps its own explanatory banner — they all carry one, and they should.
pairModes.independent: The two copies legitimately differ. No cross-repo equality is asserted; the digests still pin each side so a one-sided edit is visible. `expectedCodeDiffLines` bounds how far apart they are allowed to drift.

files.why: Both repos price the same proposals off the same `brackets` table — capucor.com when a lead builds one, capucor.app when staff amend one. Drift means two different quotes for one selection.

Both repos price the same proposals off the same `brackets` table. It carried three sanctioned divergent lines until 2026-08-06 — capucor-os logged the bracket-fetch failure through `lib/log.ts`, capucor-web through console.error — and giving capucor-web the same `lib/log.ts` collapsed that to zero. A BOUNDED divergence still needs a reader to judge whether the bound is measuring the right thing; an equality does not.

PRICING_ADDONS is the server-side WHITELIST of accepted add-on slugs and their prices, not display strings. Reprice an add-on in one repo only and the two apps quote different totals, or one silently drops an add-on the other charges for.

Both repos mint into the SAME unique client_orgs.slug column from two different Workers. A divergence in the slugify rule or the collision suffix surfaces as a unique-constraint violation on a paying client's first insert.

The retry runner in capucor-os rebuilds a capucor-web message from this file and sends it under the ORIGINAL idempotency key. A divergence means the retry sends different content from the original, inside Resend's 24-hour idempotency window.

knownDuplicates.why: Same-path files that are identical in both repos but are not worth the friction of a pinned digest — design primitives, thin client factories, and generated types. The audit still enforces the declared relationship across repos. Its real job is the INVERSE check: an identical same-path file that appears in neither this list nor handSynced is reported, so a new accidental duplicate has to be classified rather than quietly accumulate.

entries.why: shadcn/Base-Nova primitives. Drift is a visual inconsistency between the marketing site and the OS, not a data bug — but the two surfaces are meant to look like one product.
The service-role and cookieless client factories. Both repos read the same tables under the same policies; a divergence here is a silent-zero-rows bug.
One-time link tokens minted by capucor-web and consumed by flows both repos touch.
cn() plus firstOfNextMonth(), which decides the first debit date shown on a proposal and written into a subscription period.
The per-IP token bucket. Namespacing rules differ per repo but the bucket implementation must not.
On Cloudflare the real client IP is CF-Connecting-IP; x-forwarded-for is the worker loopback and collapses every visitor into one bucket. Both repos rate-limit and both record signer IPs.

Structured one-line-JSON logging into Workers Logs. `evt` is treated as an API — a saved Cloudflare query built on one repo's event name should mean the same thing in the other. It sits here rather than in handSynced deliberately: a one-sided edit is a log line in the wrong shape, not a wrong price or a broken seam, and PH-10 kept digests to the five files where a one-sided edit costs money. Cross-repo equality is still enforced.

The scheduled-workflow watchdog, byte-identical in both repos because each copy selects its own crons from scheduledWorkflows by GITHUB_REPOSITORY. A one-sided edit means one repo's crons stop being watched — caught here, cross-repo, with no digest to re-record every time the script is touched.

The deploy-drift check (R-12a), byte-identical in both repos because each copy checks its own repo, selected from deployDrift.deployments by GITHUB_REPOSITORY. A one-sided edit means one surface stops being watched for shipping behind master — caught here, cross-repo, with no digest to re-record every time the script is touched.

The CI-silence check (R-12b), byte-identical in both repos because each copy checks its own repo, selected from ciSilence.branches by GITHUB_REPOSITORY. A one-sided edit means one repo stops being watched for commits that landed with no validation run — caught here, cross-repo, with no digest to re-record every time the script is touched.

The workflow that hosts all three watchdog checks — cron silence, deploy drift and CI silence. It was already byte-identical in both repos by convention; declared 2026-08-25, when it became the host of a third control, so a one-sided edit to a trigger, a permission or an `if: always()` is caught cross-repo instead of quietly leaving one repo unwatched.
The PH-08b body cap. Per-route limits differ; the content-length-then-running-count helper must not.
The HMAC that gates detailed /api/health. Both CI workflows sign with the same scheme; a divergence silently drops one repo back to the public view.
Generated from ONE Supabase project by `npm run db:types`. If the two copies differ, one repo regenerated after a migration and the other did not — which is the only way this file can drift at all.

Toolchain configuration. Both Workers are built by the same pinned Next/OpenNext pair, so a divergence here means one repo is being linted, styled or bundled differently from the thing it is supposed to be identical to.

The same incremental-cache override in both, but the COMMENTS deliberately differ: capucor-web's describes real ISR on / and /pricing, while capucor-os's records that the same comment was copied over in Phase 1a and was false there — no /api/revalidate, and `revalidate` is banned on every per-user route. Each Worker must keep its OWN KV namespace regardless; both apps have a "/" route key, so a shared one makes one app serve the other's cached page.
Shared URLs and senders, but each repo declares its own origin defaults.
Phase 3 dropped the OS-only types (SubscriptionSummary, SubscriptionStatus, ProposalRow) from capucor-web's copy. Only the pricing shapes are shared — this is no longer a straight mirror.

syncedTriples.why: Files that must be identical in all three repos. Checked repo-to-repo by the cross-repo audit only; a digest recorded inside a file cannot cover that file itself.

routeSeam.why: One Worker per domain, split by host-based redirects, with each repo holding one half of the table. A path dropped from the wrong list turns an old bookmark or an already-sent email link into a 404.

os.note: /proposal/:path* is the one that looks removable and is not: the signing document lives on capucor.com, but proposal links in already-sent emails were minted against capucor.app.

routeSeam.forbiddenWhy: A 301 on a POST downgrades it to GET and drops the body. Redirecting /_next or /brand off capucor.app strips the CSS and logo from every portal page — which is why the lists are explicit rather than a negative-lookahead catch-all.

backup.why: The dump is the only copy of the signed debit-order mandates. Supabase Free includes no platform backups and no PITR.
keyPrefixDeclaredIn: Cloudflare R2 lifecycle rule — 185-day expiry (dashboard only, NOT checkable from here)
Cloudflare R2 bucket-lock rule — 180-day retention (dashboard only, NOT checkable from here)
backup.keyPrefixWarning: One fact in three places and only the code half is testable. Changing KEY_PREFIX without changing both Cloudflare rules silently un-retains and un-expires every object.
backup.zeroDependencyWhy: These jobs are checkout + setup-node + `node script.mjs` BY DESIGN. No `npm ci`, which is the difference between a run billing one minute against the free 2,000 and billing five. Do not add one.
backup.weakestLink: The dump exists only if cron-backup.yml keeps running, and a workflow that stops running produces an empty Actions history nobody looks at. That is now watched — see `scheduledWorkflows` below. What remains unwatchable from inside these repos is the quiet period itself: the watchdog runs on push, so it reports the silence on the first push back rather than during it.
backup.localDumpLocation: capucor-os/scripts/backup-dir.mjs, overridable with CAPUCOR_BACKUP_DIR (unset in CI, which keeps the in-repo default).
backup.localDumpLocationWhy: FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-06. The dev box's checkout is at C:\Users\zjak\OneDrive\Documents\..., so the gitignored `backups/` directory was syncing every local dump to OneDrive — seven of them, each holding the 32 signed debit-order mandates with signature images, signer IPs, SARS numbers and POPIA consent records. Not a breach (Zjak's own Microsoft account) but an unstated third-party processing location that no document mentioned and that the R2 retention story said nothing about. ⚠️ THE TRANSFERABLE LESSON: gitignoring a directory keeps it out of git and does NOTHING about a sync client, and every document here said 'gitignored, keep it off GitHub' as though those were the same statement. Zjak's decision 2026-08-06: move the directory outside the synced tree, keep all seven dumps. CAPUCOR_BACKUP_DIR now points at C:/Users/zjak/capucor-backups. ⚠️ RESIDUAL: OneDrive keeps deleted files in its cloud recycle bin for roughly 30 days, so the synced copies persist there until they age out or are purged by hand.
backup.localDumpsAreNotARetentionTier: Local dumps are a convenience for taking a snapshot before a risky migration. They are NOT one of the two backup destinations — those are the GitHub Actions artifact and the R2 object, both produced by cron-backup.yml on a runner, neither of which reads this directory. Deleting every local dump loses nothing that matters.

scheduledWorkflows.why: Everything irreplaceable here is kept alive by a GitHub Actions cron: the daily database dump (both destinations), the email/fulfilment reconciler, and the POPIA lead prune. They all fail the same way — they stop, and nothing says so. `scripts/schedule-watchdog.mjs` asks the Actions API when each one last SUCCEEDED and fails the build when the answer is older than `maxAgeDays`.
scheduledWorkflows.watchesForSilenceNotCause: The check is deliberately cause-agnostic. Asking 'is the workflow disabled?' covers one failure mode; asking 'when did it last succeed?' covers that one plus an expired secret, an exhausted Actions allowance, a renamed file, a deleted schedule and a job that has been failing every night. A watchdog written against a named cause stops working the moment the cause is different.
scheduledWorkflows.inactivityRule: MEASURED 2026-08-06, and it corrects a claim that was carried in three places. GitHub's documentation scopes the auto-disable to public repositories: 'In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days.' capucor-webpage IS public (unauthenticated api.github.com read → 200), so its two crons are exposed to exactly that rule. capucor-os is PRIVATE (→ 404) and holds cron-backup.yml, so the 60-day rule as documented does not reach the backup at all. The private repo's analogous silent-stop risk is different — it bills against a finite free Actions allowance that a public repo does not have. Neither repo is safe by being the other kind, which is why the watchdog checks recency rather than visibility.
scheduledWorkflows.cannotFireDuringQuiet: The watchdog runs on push. It cannot fire during the quiet period that causes the disable, and no in-repo mechanism can — every in-repo mechanism is hosted by the thing that goes quiet. Stated rather than papered over, with the one external control, in capucor-docs/operations/backup-watchdog.md.
scheduledWorkflows.watchdogWhy: Both copies are byte-identical and each watches only its OWN repo's crons, selected by matching GITHUB_REPOSITORY against githubRepos. A CI job cannot read a sibling repo's Actions API with its own GITHUB_TOKEN, so one watchdog covering both repos would need a cross-repo PAT — a long-lived credential to avoid duplicating a 250-line file. Two copies, no credential.

workflows.why: This is the ONLY backup of the signed debit-order mandates — Supabase Free has no platform backups and no PITR. If it has stopped, both destinations have stopped with it.

Drains durable email and signed-proposal fulfilment retries. If it has stopped, a paying client's portal stage retries forever and no email is ever resent. TWO CRONS, and the declared one is deliberately the SPARSER: `*/10 5-15 * * 1-5` is a dense weekday window sized for proposal fulfilment, and `0 * * * *` is an hourly sweep that runs every hour of every day. maxAgeDays is a STALENESS bound, so it is set against the always-on tier, which is why three is now correct where five was right for a weekday-only cadence. WARNING: the audit asserts the declared string with a SUBSTRING match, so adding a third cron would pass silently and understate the cadence — update this field whenever a cron is added, removed or retimed. The hourly tier was added 2026-08-25 under ADR 0015 PQ-3: before it, a send failing at 18:00 on a Friday waited until Monday 07:00, roughly 61 hours, while the work item stayed open.
The POPIA retention job. If it has stopped, personal data is being kept past the retention policy — a compliance failure whose only symptom is nothing happening.
Flips proposals past expires_at to expired. If it has stopped, an expired quote stays signable at a price that is no longer offered.

⚠️ THE WATCHDOG WATCHING ITS OWN SCHEDULE, AND IT IS NOT THE REGRESS watchdogWhy REFUSES. watchdog.yml runs on push (the cron and deploy-drift checks) AND on a schedule (the CI-silence check, R-12b). Those are two INDEPENDENT GitHub dispatch paths, and the 2026-08-06 incident is the evidence that they fail independently: webhook delivery was throttled to ~15% while every scheduled run fired on time. So the push half asserts the schedule half is alive (this entry) and the schedule half asserts the push half is alive (ciSilence). Mutual, not recursive — a second cron watching the FIRST cron would have shared its failure mode, which is what watchdogWhy refuses. ⚠️ It degrades gracefully in the one direction that could go quiet: if this schedule is auto-disabled by 60-day inactivity, the push half reports it on the next push — and the next push is precisely when CI silence starts mattering again. `event: "schedule"` is required here; see eventWhy.

⚠️ THE WATCHDOG WATCHING ITS OWN SCHEDULE, AND IT IS NOT THE REGRESS watchdogWhy REFUSES. watchdog.yml runs on push (the cron and deploy-drift checks) AND on a schedule (the CI-silence check, R-12b). Those are two INDEPENDENT GitHub dispatch paths, and the 2026-08-06 incident is the evidence that they fail independently: webhook delivery was throttled to ~15% while every scheduled run fired on time. So the push half asserts the schedule half is alive (this entry) and the schedule half asserts the push half is alive (ciSilence). Mutual, not recursive — a second cron watching the FIRST cron would have shared its failure mode, which is what watchdogWhy refuses. ⚠️ It degrades gracefully in the one direction that could go quiet: if this schedule is auto-disabled by 60-day inactivity, the push half reports it on the next push — and the next push is precisely when CI silence starts mattering again. `event: "schedule"` is required here; see eventWhy.

scheduledWorkflows.notBeforeWhy: ⚠️ A BOUNDED GRACE, NOT A MUTE, AND IT EXPIRES BY DATE. A workflow declared in the same change that creates its schedule has not run yet, so the watchdog would fail on it from the moment the change merges until the schedule first fires — every push red for a reason whose only fix is to wait. `notBefore` is the deadline by which the first SUCCESSFUL run must exist; until then the row reports as pending, and after it the row fails normally. ⚠️ The audit refuses a `notBefore` more than three days in the future, so this cannot be extended into an indefinite way of silencing a dead cron. 2026-08-27T06:00:00Z is the SECOND scheduled 06:00Z run after a 2026-08-25 merge, so there is one spare run in hand — GitHub delays scheduled runs, and this estate has measured that delay at up to ~2h50m. ⚠️ It sits inside the audit's own three-day bound. A first attempt used 2026-08-28 against a two-day bound and was refused on 2026-08-25 — the guard working, and the reason the bound is three rather than two: a bound equal to the date it checks goes red on the minute, which is a gate somebody widens in a hurry rather than thinks about.
scheduledWorkflows.eventWhy: ⚠️ OPTIONAL PER-ENTRY `event` FILTER, ADDED 2026-08-25 FOR R-12b, AND IT IS LOAD-BEARING ON EXACTLY ONE ENTRY. scripts/schedule-watchdog.mjs asks the Actions API for the newest successful run of a workflow WITHOUT filtering by trigger, which is correct for the four cron files above because a schedule is the only thing that runs them. watchdog.yml is different: it runs on BOTH push and schedule, so an unfiltered query would let a push run satisfy its own staleness check and a dead schedule would be invisible behind the very pushes it is meant to outlive. Setting `event: "schedule"` makes the question "has the SCHEDULE fired", which is the question that matters. Entries with no `event` behave exactly as before — the addition is a query-string suffix, not a change of semantics.
scheduledWorkflows.maxAgeWhy: Three days for a daily job, not one. GitHub delays scheduled runs under load — measured on capucor-webpage 2026-08-06, jobs scheduled for 03:15/03:30 UTC actually ran between 06:01 and 06:44 — and a run can be skipped outright. A threshold that goes red on one late night is a threshold somebody switches off.
scheduledWorkflows.reportsFailureDoesNotFailOnIt: A failing LATEST run is reported as context but is not itself a failure here. GitHub already emails on a failed scheduled run, so a red night is loud without us; silence is what nothing else covers, and a job that keeps failing crosses the staleness threshold on its own. Failing on it would also leave every push red after an intentional R2 fire drill until the next nightly run.
scheduledWorkflows.drill: SCHEDULE_WATCHDOG_DRILL=stale forces maxAgeDays to 0 so a healthy cron reads as overdue; =disabled rewrites the reported state to disabled_inactivity. Both are workflow_dispatch inputs on watchdog.yml, touch no secret and mutate nothing. Same reasoning as R2_FIRE_DRILL: an unexercised failure path is not a control.

deployDrift.why: R-12. Nothing watched capucor-os `master` drifting ahead of what is actually deployed, and on 2026-08-24 it drifted by two merges before being closed by hand. ADR 0010 part 1 made this the NORMAL state rather than an exception: deployment is now a manual dispatch on both surfaces, so a merged fix is no longer a shipped fix and drift no longer self-corrects. `scripts/deploy-drift.mjs` asks the Actions API for the newest SUCCESSFUL run of each repo's deploy workflow, takes its `head_sha`, and compares that commit to the tip of the release branch.
deployDrift.measuredEvidence: MEASURED 2026-08-24, and it is why this exists rather than being proposed. capucor-webpage's last successful production deploy was `f99bc85` at 14:20Z on 2026-08-20 — the ADR 0010 verification dispatch. `master` was `3896e1c`, `ahead_by` 21, including the Node 24 Actions upgrade and four `db.ts` regenerations. Four days, twenty-one commits, no signal anywhere. The gap this check closes was open and occupied at the moment the check was written.
deployDrift.questionIsComparisonNotAge: ⚠️ THE OBVIOUS SHAPE IS WRONG. The cron watchdog beside this asks 'when did the workflow last succeed?' and that question does not transfer. A deploy is not scheduled and has no cadence it is supposed to keep, so an age threshold on the WORKFLOW silently invents a release cadence ADR 0010 deliberately declined to set — and it is reset by a deploy that happened for an unrelated reason while the drift that matters persists. The question here is a COMPARISON: is the deployed commit still the tip of the branch, and if not, how long has the oldest unshipped commit been sitting there.
deployDrift.measuresOldestUnshippedCommitNotCommitCo: The gate is the AGE OF THE OLDEST UNSHIPPED COMMIT, never `ahead_by`. Commit count is noise: twenty-one commits of generated types is not riskier than one broken route, and gating on it would go red on a busy afternoon and green on a fortnight of neglect. Age measures the thing that actually went wrong — how long a merged fix has not been a shipped fix. `ahead_by` is reported as context and must not become a threshold.
deployDrift.equalityWouldBeSwitchedOff: ⚠️ AND IT MUST NOT BE AN EQUALITY CHECK. Under ADR 0010 `master` ahead of production is the normal state, so a check that fails whenever the deployed SHA is not the tip goes red on every single merge. The contract already learned this one for the crons — see `scheduledWorkflows.maxAgeWhy` — and the lesson is the same: a threshold that cries wolf is a threshold somebody switches off, which is how a control becomes a comment.
deployDrift.githubReposWhy: The owner/name slugs are NOT repeated here. They are already canonical in `scheduledWorkflows.githubRepos`, and a second copy is a second thing to forget when a repo is renamed. `scripts/deploy-drift.mjs` resolves this pointer rather than carrying its own map.
deployDrift.hostedByTheWatchdogWorkflow: It is a second STEP in watchdog.yml, not a second workflow. Same trigger (push), same reason (a push is the one moment we know a human is present), same zero-dependency rule, and the permissions it needs are already granted there: `actions: read` for the run, `contents: read` for the compare. No new workflow, no new credential, no new infrastructure and no additional Actions minutes — two extra API calls in a job that already runs.
deployDrift.bothCopiesIdentical: Both copies are byte-identical and each checks only its OWN repo, selected by matching GITHUB_REPOSITORY against githubRepos — exactly as the cron watchdog does, and for the same reason: a CI job cannot read a sibling repo's Actions API with its own GITHUB_TOKEN, so one copy covering both repos would need a long-lived cross-repo PAT. Two copies, no credential. Enforced by the `scripts/deploy-drift.mjs` entry in knownDuplicates.

deployments.why: capucor.app — the client portal and internal command centre. Unshipped commits here are unshipped fixes to a surface real clients sign in to, and since ADR 0003 split validation from deployment nothing ships without a human dispatching it.

capucor.com — the marketing funnel that mints proposals. This is the repo the 2026-08-24 measurement found four days and twenty-one commits adrift, and the repo whose deploy.yml has been dispatched exactly once since ADR 0010 part 1 created it.

deployDrift.maxAgeWhy: Seven days, and the number is a judgement rather than a measurement. capucor-webpage's four-day drift on 2026-08-24 was deliberate — deploy.yml was awaiting an intentional deployment — and going red on it would have been noise. The capucor.com incident of 2026-08-06 ran to two weeks and was plainly not fine. Seven splits them and turns a merged-but-unshipped fix red inside one working week. ⚠️ It is deliberately LOOSE: set tight enough to force a deploy schedule this stops being a hygiene check and becomes a release cadence, which is an amendment to ADR 0010 and belongs there rather than here.
deployDrift.cannotSeeProduction: ⚠️ IT DOES NOT OBSERVE PRODUCTION, and the distinction matters. A green deploy run proves `wrangler` uploaded a build; it does not prove the Worker is serving that code. A rollback in the Cloudflare dashboard, a hand-run `npx wrangler deploy` from a laptop, or a deploy that succeeded against the wrong account are all invisible from the Actions API. True ground truth would need the deployed app to advertise its build SHA and this job to fetch it — but the detailed /api/health response is HMAC-signed with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, and putting a production secret into a job that runs on EVERY push is a worse trade than the gap it closes. Stated rather than papered over.
deployDrift.cannotFireDuringQuiet: Same limit as the cron watchdog, and sharper here, because a push is the very thing that CREATES drift. A repo that goes quiet while drifted stays silent until someone pushes again. The 2026-08-24 measurement is the worked example: capucor-webpage's drift began on 2026-08-20 and would have been reported on the next push, four days later — loudly, and four days before anyone found it by hand.
deployDrift.cannotJudgeWhetherDriftMatters: Twenty-one commits of generated types and one broken route look identical from here. This check reports that production is not the tip and how long that has been true; deciding whether it matters is a human reading the commit list.
deployDrift.closesOnlyTheDriftHalf: ⚠️ IT CLOSES ONLY THE DRIFT HALF OF R-12. The risk records two gaps: deploy drift, and CI SILENCE — the 2026-08-06 incident in which GitHub dropped push triggers on capucor-webpage so ci.yml never ran at all. This check does not detect that, and cannot: it is hosted by the push trigger that goes missing. R-12a is this. R-12b is CI silence, and it is closed separately by `ciSilence` — which is hosted on the SCHEDULE for exactly that reason, and whose theDetectorIsNotSelfReferential records why the self-referential framing this note used to carry was wrong.
deployDrift.drill: DEPLOY_DRIFT_DRILL=drift rewrites the observed comparison to 99 commits ahead with an oldest unshipped commit 99 days old, so the common failure and its message are exercised against the REAL API; =never rewrites the observed run to absent, exercising the 'this repo has never deployed' path. Both are workflow_dispatch inputs on watchdog.yml, touch no secret and mutate nothing. Same reasoning as SCHEDULE_WATCHDOG_DRILL and R2_FIRE_DRILL: an unexercised failure path is not a control. The drill forces the CONDITION true rather than moving the threshold, because with the deployed SHA at the tip there is no unshipped commit for a threshold of zero to act on.

ciSilence.why: R-12b. Nothing watched for CI SILENCE — commits landing on the release branch with no validation run at all. On 2026-08-06 a GitHub Actions incident (impact: critical, 15:05Z → 00:14Z; GitHub's own 20:34Z status update reads "webhook triggers are currently throttled to help with recovery and we are processing approximately 15% of webhooks, so many events such as pushes and pull requests are not triggering new workflow runs") dropped two pushes to capucor-webpage. `4283406` at 21:01:33Z and `56e0acf` at 21:50:33Z produced NO workflow runs of any kind. The crons stayed green, nothing went red, and capucor.com sat three commits behind master for two weeks. The gap was found by hand on 2026-08-20, not by a control.
ciSilence.theDetectorIsNotSelfReferential: ⚠️ THIS CORRECTS THE RISK REGISTER'S OWN FRAMING, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. R-12b recorded the difficulty as "any in-repo check for 'did CI run on this commit?' is hosted by the same push trigger that was dropped". That is true of a PUSH-hosted check and FALSE of a SCHEDULE-hosted one. MEASURED 2026-08-25 against the Actions API for the incident window: cron-prune-leads.yml ran 2026-08-07 05:03:01Z (schedule, success, head `56e0acf`) and cron-expire-proposals.yml ran 05:15:41Z (schedule, success, head `56e0acf`), while ci.yml's last push run was 2026-08-06 16:54Z on `dd3dbf4`. The schedule dispatch path stayed up throughout and ran, seven hours after the last dropped push, with the exact commit CI never validated as its head. A scheduled check asking this question would have gone red that morning instead of the gap running to a fortnight.
ciSilence.hostedOnTheScheduleNotThePush: ⚠️ IT RUNS ON THE SCHEDULE, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE CRON WATCHDOG BESIDE IT AND FOR THE OPPOSITE REASON. scheduledWorkflows.watchdogWhy refuses a cron watching a cron, because they share a failure mode. Here the thing being watched IS the push path, so hosting the detector on the push path is that same mistake and the schedule is the independent choice. It is a third STEP in watchdog.yml rather than a new workflow: a new workflow is a second thing to notice going quiet, and the permissions it needs — `actions: read` and `contents: read` — are already granted there.
ciSilence.amendsTheWatchdogsPushOnlyRule: ⚠️ THIS AMENDS A RECORDED DECISION, AND THE COMMENT WAS REWRITTEN RATHER THAN EXTENDED. watchdog.yml's header used to read "IT RUNS ON PUSH, NOT ON A SCHEDULE, and that is the whole point", which was about CRON silence and is still correct about it. The file now runs on both and says which question each trigger answers. A later reader finding the old sentence beside a `schedule:` block would reasonably assume the schedule had been added carelessly.
ciSilence.reportOnlyNeverARequiredCheck: ⚠️ REPORT-ONLY. It turns the watchdog run red; it is NOT a required status check and must not become one. Promoting it to a merge gate would change the release process — an amendment to ADR 0003 and ADR 0010 — and that belongs in those ADRs, not in a check. It would also be self-defeating: during the very incident this exists to detect, a required check that cannot run is a repository nobody can merge into.
ciSilence.asksDidItRunNotDidItPass: It asks whether validation RAN, never whether it passed. A failing run is loud already — GitHub emails on it — and a red CI is somebody's problem within the hour. Silence produces no run, therefore no failure, therefore no email, and that is the thing nothing else covers. Same division of labour as scheduledWorkflows.reportsFailureDoesNotFailOnIt.
ciSilence.firstParentOnly: ⚠️ IT WALKS THE FIRST-PARENT CHAIN FROM THE TIP, NOT EVERY ANCESTOR, AND CHECKING EVERY ANCESTOR WOULD BE RED ON A HEALTHY REPO WITHIN A DAY. Both repos merge pull requests as merge commits, so a push to master creates ONE ci.yml run whose head_sha is the merge commit. The commits inside the merged branch are ancestors of master that were never the head of a push to it — they were validated by `pull_request` runs, under a different head. The first-parent chain is exactly the set of commits a push trigger was owed. On a squash-merge repo the chain is every commit, so this degrades correctly rather than silently narrowing.
ciSilence.githubReposWhy: The owner/name slugs are NOT repeated here, for the same reason deployDrift does not repeat them: a second copy is a second thing to forget when a repo is renamed. `scripts/ci-silence.mjs` resolves this pointer.
ciSilence.hostedByTheWatchdogWorkflow: A third STEP in watchdog.yml, after the cron watchdog and the deploy-drift check, and carrying `if: always()` for the same reason they do: without it a failure in either step above skips this one, so the three verdicts could never be seen in the same run and the louder would mask the quieter.
ciSilence.bothCopiesIdentical: Both copies are byte-identical and each checks only its OWN repo, selected by matching GITHUB_REPOSITORY against githubRepos — exactly as the cron watchdog and the drift check do, and for the same reason: a CI job cannot read a sibling repo's Actions API with its own GITHUB_TOKEN, so one copy covering both repos would need a long-lived cross-repo PAT. Two copies, no credential. Enforced by the `scripts/ci-silence.mjs` entry in knownDuplicates.

branches.why: capucor.app — the client portal and internal command centre. A commit that landed here without validation is a commit deploy.yml will happily ship on the next dispatch, because deploy.yml re-runs the gates against the tip rather than against each commit.
capucor.com — the marketing funnel that mints proposals, and the repo the 2026-08-06 incident actually hit. Two pushes here were validated by nothing and nobody knew for two weeks.

ciSilence.graceWhy: Six hours before a commit is expected to have a run, and the number is a judgement rather than a measurement. A run normally appears within seconds, so a grace of minutes would be enough on a healthy day — but GitHub's own delays on this estate have been measured in hours (jobs scheduled for 03:15 and 03:30 UTC ran between 06:01 and 06:44 on 2026-08-06), and this check runs daily, so buying quiet at the cost of six hours of detection latency costs nothing real. ⚠️ Without a grace window every commit pushed in the minutes before the cron fires reads as unvalidated, the check goes red for reasons nobody can act on, and a gate that cries wolf is a gate somebody switches off.
ciSilence.lookbackWhy: Fourteen days, chosen against the incident it exists to catch: the 2026-08-06 gap ran to exactly two weeks before a human found it. A window shorter than the known failure would let the same event age out of view before anyone looked. It is a WINDOW, not a threshold — a commit older than this is not forgiven, it is simply no longer reported, and the deploy-drift check beside this one is what notices an old unshipped commit.
ciSilence.cannotSurviveATotalActionsOutage: ⚠️ A TOTAL ACTIONS OUTAGE TAKES BOTH PATHS. Schedules survived the 2026-08-06 incident; that is evidence, not a guarantee. If Actions is wholly down nothing in-repo runs, and the control for that is the external one in capucor-docs/operations/backup-watchdog.md — the same shape, and the same admission, as the backup residual.
ciSilence.cannotSeePullRequests: ⚠️ IT WATCHES THE RELEASE BRANCH ONLY. A dropped `pull_request` trigger — where CI actually gates a merge — is invisible here. Deliberately out of the first cut: an un-run PR check leaves the pull request visibly un-green in front of the person merging it, which is a signal a dropped push trigger on master does not have.
ciSilence.detectionIsSameDayNotImmediate: ⚠️ ONE CRON INTERVAL, PLUS GitHub's scheduling delay — measured on this estate at up to ~2h50m. This shortens the 2026-08-06 gap from a fortnight to a day. It does not make it zero, and nothing hosted inside these repos can.
ciSilence.provesARunExistedNotThatItWasHonest: ⚠️ It proves a run EXISTED, not that the run was honest. A ci.yml gutted to `run: true` still produces a run. Same class of limit as deployDrift.cannotSeeProduction, and stated rather than papered over.
ciSilence.lastReviewedNotBumped: ⚠️ `lastReviewed` is deliberately NOT bumped by this 2026-08-25 addition, for the same reason it was not bumped when deployDrift landed: only the CI-observability area was reviewed, not the whole manifest. A full contract review remains unscheduled.
ciSilence.narrowsTheQuietPeriodResidual: ⚠️ A SIDE EFFECT WORTH STATING PRECISELY, BECAUSE IT IS EASY TO OVERCLAIM. Adding a schedule to watchdog.yml means the CRON watchdog step now also runs daily, not only on push — so scheduledWorkflows.cannotFireDuringQuiet is NARROWED. It is not closed, and the two repos differ: capucor-os is PRIVATE, GitHub's 60-day inactivity disable does not reach it, and its backup cron is therefore genuinely watched through a quiet period now. capucor-webpage is PUBLIC, so after 60 days of inactivity watchdog.yml's own schedule is auto-disabled along with everything else and the residual returns in full. The external calendar reminder in capucor-docs/operations/backup-watchdog.md is still the control for that, and this addition does not retire it.
ciSilence.drill: CI_SILENCE_DRILL=silent removes the run belonging to the OLDEST in-window commit, so one commit reads as validated by nothing while the rest stay healthy — the 2026-08-06 shape exactly, two pushes lost out of many. =blind rewrites the commit list to empty, exercising the 'I could not enumerate the branch' path, which MUST fail rather than pass green. Both are workflow_dispatch inputs on watchdog.yml, touch no secret and mutate nothing. Both force the CONDITION true rather than moving a threshold, for the same reason DEPLOY_DRIFT_DRILL does: on a healthy repo every commit has a run, so a threshold-moving drill would have nothing to act on and would pass green — and a drill that cannot fail is the bug it exists to catch, one level up.

migrationLedger.evidence: Until 2026-08-06 the ledger SCHEMA did not exist — `select count(*) from information_schema.schemata where schema_name = 'supabase_migrations'` returned 0, measured read-only on 2026-08-05 and again immediately before the repair. The repair created it with `supabase migration repair --status applied` (the CLI's own command, so the DDL is the CLI's and not hand-rolled) and backfilled the 21 CLI-parseable versions 001-008 and 010-022. `supabase db push --dry-run` now reports `Remote database is up to date`. The schema was proven unmoved either side: `npm run db:check` passed 27 tables from 23 migrations, and `npm run db:types` regenerated with NO diff against the committed src/types/db.ts.
migrationLedger.pushAllowedWhy: Reviewed and approved by Zjak on 2026-08-06, then executed against a proven backup. The ban existed because a 2026-08-04 dry run proposed replaying every plain `create table` migration from 001 against a live database that already had all 27 tables. With the ledger honest, the dry run proposes nothing. `npm run db:check` remains the gate that actually proves the result and still runs in CI — db push replaces the apply step, not the proof. NOTE: the original approval also cited 'db diff becomes usable' as a benefit. That turned out to be FALSE on this machine — see driftDetection. The audit trail and the honest ledger are the real payoff; the drift half was solved a different way.
migrationLedger.driftDetection: MEASURED 2026-08-06. `supabase db diff` — the tool for catching a change made out of band in the Supabase dashboard — is NOT reachable from the dev box. It needs a shadow database, which needs Docker, which is not installed; the command dies at 'Creating shadow database'. Three options were weighed: install Docker Desktop locally (heavy, licensing question, and only runs when someone remembers), run `db diff` in CI (a runner has Docker, but `--linked` needs the production DATABASE PASSWORD as a repo secret — a credential neither repo holds and strictly more powerful than the service-role key), or take the affordable subset. Zjak chose the subset. `scripts/check-schema-drift.mjs` now checks BOTH directions using the PostgREST OpenAPI document it was already fetching: migrations ⊆ live (the original gate) and live ⊆ migrations (undeclared objects). Zero new credentials, zero new infrastructure, runs in the CI gate that already exists. Proven clean against production on 2026-08-06 and drilled by removing migration 017 locally — it reported all seven register tables as undeclared and exited 1.
migrationLedger.driftDetectionLimits: The reverse direction sees TABLES AND COLUMNS ONLY. Triggers, functions, RLS policies and constraints stay invisible — the same blind spot `db:check` always had, now stated rather than implied. A dashboard-added trigger or a loosened policy is still uncatchable from here. ⛔ Do not describe the reverse check as a replacement for `db diff`; it is the part of `db diff` that a machine without Docker can afford. If that residual ever needs closing, the honest options are the two that were declined above, and the CI one costs a production database password.
migrationLedger.ledgerInvariant: Every version in the remote ledger MUST have a matching local migration file. A remote-only version is not harmlessly ignored: `supabase db push` aborts with 'Remote migration versions not found in local migrations directory' and EVERY push stays blocked until the row is removed. MEASURED 2026-08-06 on CLI 2.93.1 — the repair first backfilled 0091/0092 for the two 009 files, and the dry run refused to run at all. This is why the two files below are deliberately absent from the ledger.
migrationLedger.filenamePatternWhy: The Supabase CLI parses a migration version as the leading digits up to the first underscore. A letter-suffixed name is not merely mis-ordered — the file is not treated as a migration at all. The CLI does print `Skipping migration <file>... (file name must match pattern)`, so it is visible if you read the output, but nothing fails.
migrationLedger.knownNonConformingWhy: There were two 009_ files until 2026-08-03. They were suffixed rather than renumbered so the file order still reflects when they were actually applied. They are applied in the database and are deliberately NOT in the ledger: the CLI cannot see the files, so it will never propose them, and recording them by hand blocks every push (see ledgerInvariant). Decided 2026-08-06 — the ledger's two-row hole lives in prose here rather than renaming files that four documents reference. If they are ever renumbered to conforming names, backfill the matching versions in the SAME change.

fixedPaths.why: The three SessionStart hooks in .claude/hooks/ read these files by hard-coded path and grep for a control line, and the two per-repo settings.json files are what makes those hooks RUN at all for a session started inside a repo. Moving or renaming any of them breaks the nudge SILENTLY — the hook exits 0 on a missing file by design, and a settings.json pointing at a script bash cannot find produces no error a person ever sees. Nothing else in the estate reports it, which is why it is pinned here.

entries.readBy: Claude Code, for any session started in capucor-os/
entries.why: ADDED 2026-08-25 by WC-04. Claude Code does not read settings.json from parent directories — MEASURED, not assumed: before this file existed, a headless session started in capucor-os/ ran ZERO SessionStart hooks while one started at the workspace root ran the root’s. Most work happens in this repo, so every nudge was dead exactly where it was needed. ⚠️ THE ../ IN THAT COMMAND ESCAPES THE REPOSITORY ON PURPOSE, so the hook scripts exist once rather than three times. If the workspace is ever restructured so this repo is not a direct child of the folder holding .claude/hooks/, bash cannot find the script and the nudge dies with no error anywhere.

entries.readBy: Claude Code, for any session started in capucor-web/
entries.why: ADDED 2026-08-25 by WC-04, same mechanism as capucor-os. ⚠️ capucor-webpage is a PUBLIC repository and this file is committed: it must never carry a secret, a token, a project id or an absolute local path. Review it as if a stranger will read it, because one can.

workspaceRootSentinel.why: ⚠️ EVERY SessionStart hook root-anchors itself by walking UP from the session’s project directory until it finds a folder with this name, then cd’s there so its root-relative reads resolve. RENAME OR MOVE capucor-docs/ AND EVERY HOOK GOES SILENT AT ONCE — the walk-up fails, the hook exits 0, and nothing anywhere reports it. That is the single highest-blast-radius rename in the workspace, and it is why this is a contract key rather than only a comment in the scripts. The walk stops at a FIXPOINT, not at "/": on Windows, dirname of "c:" is "c:", so the obvious "/" guard never terminates for a session started outside the workspace and the hook would HANG session start rather than exit quietly. Measured in Git Bash 2026-08-25.
workspaceRootSentinel.unversionedWhy: Those three paths are at the WORKSPACE ROOT, which is not a git repo and cannot be one — it holds the three repos. They are versioned in capucor-docs/workspace-root/dot-claude/hooks/ and deployed by capucor-docs/workspace-root/bootstrap.sh. The audit checks the DEPLOYED copies, because those are the ones that actually run, and separately checks the vendored copies have not drifted from them. Nothing else detects a stale vendored copy.

rootScaffold.why: ⚠️ THE WORKSPACE ROOT IS IN NO REPOSITORY AND CANNOT BE ONE — it CONTAINS the three repos. Everything that sits there is therefore unversioned, and the only protection is the vendored mirror in capucor-docs/workspace-root/ plus bootstrap.sh. That protection was INCOMPLETE AND SILENTLY SO: bootstrap.sh mapped eight files and synced brand-assets/, and handover/ — eight briefs that existed nowhere else — was in neither. Nothing detected it, and nothing would have detected the next one. This key is the allowlist that closes the CLASS rather than the instance. The precedent is not hypothetical: the ENTIRE root scaffold went missing between 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-24 when the workspace moved and only the repos came across, taking all three SessionStart nudges and the whole audit fire drill offline for seventeen days before anyone noticed.
rootScaffold.root: the parent directory of the three repo folders
rootScaffold.allowlistNotDenylist: ⚠️ THIS IS AN ALLOWLIST, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT. A denylist assumes a new unexpected entry at the root is fine until someone names it as a problem; an allowlist assumes it is a problem until someone classifies it. handover/ survived years of denylist thinking. Every entry present at the workspace root must appear in `entries` below or the audit fails, which forces the question "is this thing versioned anywhere?" to be answered at the moment it is created.

dispositions.mirrored: Vendored in capucor-docs/workspace-root/ and restored by bootstrap.sh. Must exist at the root AND match its vendored copy BYTE-FOR-BYTE.
dispositions.superseded: Present at the root, deliberately NOT vendored, because a canonical copy already lives in a repository. `canonicalCopy` names it and the audit asserts that copy exists — a superseded classification that has itself gone stale is worse than no classification. bootstrap.sh does not restore these, so a rebuilt workspace will not have them, and that is intended.
dispositions.ignored-by-design: Present at the root and deliberately outside the mirror. The three repo folders (they version themselves) and per-machine local files.
dispositions.generated: Reproducible from something else in the estate, so neither vendored nor checked for content. ⚠️ NOTHING AT THE ROOT IS `generated` TODAY. The term is defined so that the first build artifact to appear at the root has an honest classification available and does not get quietly filed as `ignored-by-design`.

rootScaffold.byteExactWhy: ⚠️ THE COMPARISON IS BYTE-EXACT AND MUST NEVER NORMALISE LINE ENDINGS. workspace-root/** is `-text` in .gitattributes and the deployed root files are LF, while the rest of capucor-docs is CRLF in this Windows worktree. A comparison that normalised would pass on a vendored hook that bootstrap.sh would then restore with CRLF line endings — and A CRLF `#!/usr/bin/env bash` DOES NOT EXECUTE. The check would be green and the restored workspace broken. Binary files (brand-assets/*.png) are compared the same way, which byte comparison handles and a text comparison would corrupt.
rootScaffold.degradesWhen: ⚠️ SKIP WITH A NOTE, NEVER FAIL, WHEN THE SCAFFOLD IS NOT DEPLOYED HERE. `npm run audit` is not run in CI — it needs all three repos and the unversioned root — but it CAN legitimately be run in a bare workspace: three repos freshly cloned into an empty folder, before anyone has run bootstrap.sh. In that shape every mirrored entry is absent, which is a workspace that has not been bootstrapped yet, not drift. The rule is ALL-OR-NOTHING: if ZERO mirrored entries are present the check emits a NOTE telling the reader to run bootstrap.sh and stops. If SOME are present and some are not, that is a partially-deployed root and it FAILS. A check that fails for structural reasons is a check that gets switched off, and a check that stays quiet when half the scaffold is missing is not a check at all.
rootScaffold.vendorOnlyWhy: The only two files allowed to live in capucor-docs/workspace-root/ WITHOUT being deployed to the root: the mirror’s own documentation and its restore script. ⚠️ ANYTHING ELSE VENDORED THERE AND NOT NAMED BY AN ENTRY BELOW IS A FILE SOMEONE MEANT TO PUT AT THE ROOT AND DID NOT WIRE UP — it looks protected, bootstrap.sh never copies it, and a rebuilt workspace silently lacks it. That is the same silent-incompleteness failure as handover/, running in the other direction.

delegatedToDocsCheck.why: ⚠️ THESE THREE ARE ALREADY ASSERTED BYTE-FOR-BYTE AGAINST THEIR VENDORED COPIES BY THE `docs` CHECK, via fixedPaths.workspaceRootSentinel, added by WC-04. This check therefore SKIPS them rather than re-implementing the same assertion: two checks reporting one defect trains people to read the report as noise, and the second one to be written is the one that drifts. They are still `mirrored` — bootstrap.sh restores them and the drill still proves the assertion — it is only the comparison that lives elsewhere. ⚠️ IF THE SENTINEL BLOCK IS EVER REMOVED FROM fixedPaths, DELETE THIS LIST IN THE SAME CHANGE or the three highest-blast-radius files at the root become the only unchecked ones.

entries.name: AGENTS.md
entries.why: Canonical root orientation, loaded into every session started at the root. Carries the `Last reviewed` stamp self-review-nudge.sh greps for, which is also pinned in fixedPaths. ⚠️ The most common root edit by far is bumping that stamp during /self-review — mirror it.

entries.name: CLAUDE.md
entries.why: Thin pointer to AGENTS.md. Line-counted separately by docs.thinPointers.

entries.name: GEMINI.md
entries.why: Thin pointer to AGENTS.md. Also a docs.linkCheckRoot.

entries.name: .ignore
entries.why: Scopes ripgrep away from node_modules and build output for every agent working here. ⚠️ Stored dot-prefix-renamed: a real .ignore inside capucor-docs would silently change what searches in THAT repo can see.

entries.name: .claude
entries.why: Permissions and the four SessionStart hooks. ⚠️ Stored as dot-claude/ deliberately: a real .claude/ directory inside capucor-docs would be read as configuration FOR THAT REPOSITORY and its SessionStart hooks would fire in every capucor-docs session with the wrong working directory. bootstrap.sh renames on copy. The whole tree is compared, so a FOURTH hook script added at the root and not vendored fails this check — which is exactly the WC-09 shape.

exceptions.why: ⚠️ PER-MACHINE, AND IT MUST NEVER BE VENDORED. The copy on the dev box has carried allow-rules containing LIVE PROPOSAL SIGNING TOKENS from past debugging sessions; committing it would put client-facing capability tokens into git history permanently. Nothing is lost by leaving it out — Claude Code recreates it as it prompts for permissions. ⚠️ Both of the tokens found there on 2026-08-25 were already dead by TTL, which is luck, not a control.

entries.name: brand-assets
entries.why: Five PNGs, legacy convenience copies. ⚠️ RETIRING THIS FOLDER IS AN OPEN DECISION, not settled here: rules/where-things-live.md records it as "not canonical after Brand v1" and the masters now live in capucor-docs/knowledge/brand/assets/source-masters/, so vendoring these is a fourth copy of material this estate already owns. It is classified `mirrored` because that is what bootstrap.sh does TODAY and this key must describe the root as it is. Retiring it means editing the scaffold, this entry, the AGENTS.md bullet and the additionalDirectories entry in settings.json together — a brand-canonicality decision for the Brand v1 phases.

entries.name: handover
entries.why: Eight handover briefs (ADR 0010 parts 1 and 2, O-2, S-1, S-2, S-4, S-5, and an archived e2e defect brief). ⚠️ THIS FOLDER IS THE REASON THIS WHOLE KEY EXISTS — it sat at the root, in no repository and in no mirror, and nothing anywhere reported it. WC-01 rescued all eight into capucor-docs/archive/handover/ on 2026-08-25; verified line by line, each rescued copy differs from the root original by exactly the 8-line provenance banner WC-01 added and nothing else, and archive/E2E_SESSION_DEFECT_HANDOVER_BRIEF.md was flattened out of the root subfolder in the process. DOCUMENTED DECISION, Zjak, 2026-08-25: classified `superseded` rather than mirrored or deleted. Not mirrored, because vendoring it would make a THIRD copy and the vendored copy would lack the banner, so the two capucor-docs copies would disagree. Not deleted, because 00-plan.md’s standing rules make WC-06 the only chunk that deletes. ⚠️ RETIRING THE ROOT COPY IS A WC-06 CANDIDATE, and it must change this entry in the same commit — a root that no longer contains what the mirror would restore, described by a contract that still says it does, is a check contradicting itself.

entries.name: capucor-os
entries.why: ⚠️ A GIT REPOSITORY. It versions itself and MUST NEVER BE MIRRORED — nor may node_modules/, .next/ or .open-next/ inside it. Mirroring a repo into a folder inside another repo is how the retired OneDrive scaffold came to be a snapshot of a snapshot.

entries.name: capucor-web
entries.why: ⚠️ A GIT REPOSITORY (remote name: capucor-webpage, and PUBLIC). Never mirrored.

entries.name: capucor-docs
entries.why: ⚠️ A GIT REPOSITORY, and also the walk-up sentinel every SessionStart hook looks for — see fixedPaths.workspaceRootSentinel. Never mirrored; it HOLDS the mirror.

boardCoverage.why: ⚠️ Every project directory under capucor-docs/plans/ must have at least one row on the board, and every board row must resolve to a chunk file that exists. ways-of-working.md makes the board the single place to answer what’s next; a project running without a row on it is a project running outside the system, which is exactly how Phase 2 took ~20 commits, four ADRs and three T-0 merges between 2026-08-24 and 2026-08-25 with no chunk file, no board row and no handover for any of it.
boardCoverage.wouldNotHaveCaughtPhase2: ⚠️ STATED HONESTLY, BECAUSE THE OPPOSITE BELIEF IS THE DANGEROUS ONE: this check would NOT have caught the drift it was written in response to. Phase 2 had no plans/ directory AT ALL, so there was no project directory for the check to find unlisted. What it does catch is the next-cheapest failure — a project whose chunk files nobody put on the board, or a board row pointing at a file since renamed or deleted. Catching "an accepted ADR exists but no project tracks its slices" needs a judgement no script makes. This is a BACKSTOP, not the fix. The fix is that the board nudge now reaches the repo where the work happens.
boardCoverage.rowShape: A board row is a relative markdown link from capucor-docs/plans/README.md into a project directory beneath it, i.e. [text](<project>/<file>.md). Absolute URLs, bare anchors, and links that climb out of plans/ are not board rows and are ignored.

docs.why: The board, the tracker and the two AGENTS.md files are load-bearing navigation. A relative link that stopped resolving is the cheapest possible drift to catch and the easiest to leave rotting.
docs.linkCheckExcludeWhy: archive/ is frozen history. Its documents cite files at the paths they had when the work was done, and a good number of those files were deleted in Phase 3 of the OS split. Rewriting those links to today's paths would make the record say something that was never true, and deleting them would lose the citation. A link checker that forces a historical document to describe the present is a checker that gets switched off. workspace-root/ is excluded for a different reason: it is a byte-exact VENDORED COPY of the unversioned workspace-root scaffold, and its links are written to resolve from the workspace root where bootstrap.sh deploys it, not from where it is stored. Checked in place, every ./capucor-* link in the vendored AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md resolves one directory too deep and reads as broken — 31 of them when this was added. The DEPLOYED copies at the workspace root ARE checked: root 'AGENTS.md' and 'GEMINI.md' are both linkCheckRoots. So this exclusion loses no coverage; it drops a duplicate check aimed at the wrong base directory. Root GEMINI.md was ADDED to linkCheckRoots in the same change — it was only ever line-counted as a thinPointer, so its four links had never been resolved anywhere. ADDED 2026-08-24 with the scaffold itself, after it went missing for seventeen days because the workspace root is not a repo.
